01.note: Rabbi Yohanan taught that in the future God will set huge precious stones and pearls, thirty by thirty cubits with openings ten by twenty, in the gates of Jerusalem. A student sneered: we cannot even find a gem the size of a dove's egg. Later, at sea, the student saw ministering angels sawing exactly such stones and was told they were for Jerusalem's gates. He came back and told Rabbi Yohanan he had seen it just as he said. Rabbi Yohanan called him worthless, said he had believed only because he had seen and was mocking the words of the Sages, and set his eyes on him; the student was killed and turned into a pile of bones.
01.why: The Gemara is interpreting Isaiah's verses about the future glory of Jerusalem, and brings this story to explain the words "your gates of precious stones." Afterward it questions how gates ten by twenty cubits fit with teachings that people will then be a hundred cubits tall.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage teaching about the future gates of Jerusalem.

people.name: A certain student
people.about: An unnamed student who mocked Rabbi Yohanan's teaching and later saw it confirmed.

terms.meaning: Angels who serve God; here the student finds them preparing the gems for Jerusalem.
An ancient measure of length, roughly the distance from elbow to fingertip, about half a meter.

02.note: Rav Pappa had twelve thousand dinars held for him by others in Bei Hozai. He transferred ownership of that money to his agent, Rav Shmuel bar Aha, by means of the threshold of his house, so that the agent could go and collect it. When Rav Shmuel bar Aha came back with the money, Rav Pappa was so glad that he went out as far as Tavakh to greet him.
02.why: The Gemara has just said that money, which cannot be acquired by a symbolic exchange, can be transferred along with land. Rav Pappa's handing over distant money "by means of" his threshold is brought as an example of that.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Owner of money held for him in Bei Hozai.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Aha
people.about: Rav Pappa's agent, who received the money and brought it back.

terms.meaning: A legal method in which movable goods or money pass to the new owner together with a piece of land he acquires, even if the goods are far away.
A silver coin; twelve thousand dinars was a large sum.

03.note: Rabbi Yehuda reports that in Tzalmon a man planted his vineyard with sixteen cubits between rows. Each year he bent the branches of two facing rows to one side and sowed grain in the cleared strip, then switched sides the next year. The case came before the Sages and they permitted it. Separately, Rav Yosef recalls a case of trees sold in a village of shepherds that came before Rav Yehuda, who told the seller to give the buyer land "sufficient for an ox and its vessels"; Rav Yosef did not know how much that was until he heard a mishna about keeping trees four cubits from a neighbor's field.
03.why: The Gemara is asking how far apart three trees may be and still count as one unit. Abaye points to the Tzalmon ruling to support a sixteen-cubit limit, and Rav Yosef answers with Rav Yehuda's ruling, which he takes to mean four cubits.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports the Tzalmon vineyard case.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Answers Abaye by recalling a case he saw decided.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The judge who ruled in the shepherds' village case.

terms.meaning: The Torah's ban on sowing other crops in a vineyard; the Tzalmon case asks whether sowing between widely spaced rows breaks it.
The early collection of rabbinic teachings that the Gemara discusses and cites.

03.flag: The story combines two separate incidents (the Tzalmon vineyard and Rav Yosef's shepherds' village case), and Rav Yosef's account finishes in the next segment, where he concludes the measure is four cubits.

04.note: A man walked into a butcher shop and lifted a thigh of meat to look at it; while he held it, a horseman came and seized it from him. He came before Rav Yeimar, who made him pay the butcher its value. In another case, a man brought pumpkins to Pum Nahara and everyone took one without paying yet; angry, he declared the pumpkins consecrated to Heaven. They came before Rav Kahana, who said a person cannot consecrate something that is not his.
04.why: Shmuel has just ruled that one who takes a vessel from a craftsman to examine it is liable if it breaks, when its price is fixed. Both cases apply that idea: where the price is fixed, lifting the item works like completing the purchase.

people.name: Rav Yeimar
people.about: Judge who made the buyer pay for the meat seized from his hands.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Judge who ruled that the pumpkin seller's consecration had no effect.

terms.meaning: Declared the property of the Temple, so that no one else may use it.
Where an item's price is set and known, so that picking it up shows the buyer has agreed to the deal.

05.note: The house of the Nasi appointed market inspectors to supervise both measures and prices. Shmuel told his student Karna to go out and teach them that inspectors are appointed for measures but not for prices. Karna went out and taught instead that they are appointed for both. Shmuel asked his name, and when he answered "Karna," Shmuel said: let a horn grow in his eye. A growth came out in Karna's eye.
05.why: The Gemara is drawing rules from the Torah's demand for honest weights and measures, and a teaching that courts appoint inspectors for measures but not prices; the story shows Shmuel holding to that, while the Gemara says Karna followed Rabbi Yitzhak, who allows inspectors for prices too.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The teacher who sent Karna to correct the Nasi's household.

people.name: Karna
people.about: Shmuel's student, who taught the opposite of his instructions.

terms.meaning: The Patriarch, the official head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel; his household made appointments like these.
Officials who checked that merchants used accurate measures, and, in some views, fair prices.
The student's name, which also means "horn" in Aramaic; Shmuel's curse plays on it.

06.note: The sister of Rami bar Pappa was married to Rav Avya. When she died, Rav Avya performed the ceremony of standing and sitting for her. Rav Yosef said he made two mistakes: the ceremony is done only with close relatives and he did it even with distant ones, and it is done only on the first day and he did it on the second day.
06.why: The Gemara has just described the mourners' practice of stopping seven times on the way back from a burial. Rav Avya's case is used to set its limits, and Abaye and Rava go on to add further errors he made.

people.name: Rav Avya
people.about: Husband of Rami bar Pappa's sister; held the ceremony when she died.

people.name: Rami bar Pappa
people.about: Brother of Rav Avya's wife.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who said Rav Avya erred in two ways.

terms.meaning: A mourning rite in which those returning from a burial stop and sit, then stand and walk on, several times, to honor the dead.

07.note: Rav Pappa bought land from a man who told him it was a field of twenty griv. When Rav Pappa measured it, it held only fifteen. He came before Abaye, who told him: you knew what you were buying and accepted it. Rav Pappa objected that the mishna lets a buyer deduct for a shortfall; Abaye answered that this holds only for a buyer unfamiliar with the field. Rav Pappa objected that the seller had said twenty; Abaye answered that he meant the field was as good as one of twenty.
07.why: The mishna has been ruling on fields sold by stated size that turn out smaller, and the Gemara is debating exactly how much of a shortfall is allowed. Rav Pappa's case adds that a buyer who already knew the field cannot claim the difference.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Bought a field that turned out smaller than the seller said.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Judge who ruled against Rav Pappa.

terms.meaning: A measure of land by how much seed it takes to sow; twenty griv here means a field fit for twenty se'a of grain.
The early collection of rabbinic teachings; here its rule on fields sold with a stated size.

08.note: Rabbi Yannai, whose eyes were dim, walked leaning on the shoulder of his attendant Rabbi Simlai, when Rabbi Yehuda Nesia came toward them. Rabbi Simlai said the man coming was handsome and so was his cloak. When he reached them, Rabbi Yannai felt the cloak and said it was as coarse as sackcloth. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia asked how we know a son comes before a daughter in inheriting a mother's property; Rabbi Yannai derived it from a verse linking the mother's tribe to the father's. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia objected that then a firstborn should take a double portion of a mother's property too. Rabbi Yannai told his attendant: take me away, this man does not want to learn.
08.why: The Gemara has been rejecting the view that a son and daughter inherit equally from their mother. This story gives the source for a son coming first, and Abaye then answers the question Rabbi Yannai brushed aside.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: An elderly Sage with dim eyes, led by his attendant.

people.name: Rabbi Simlai
people.about: Rabbi Yannai's attendant, on whose shoulder he leaned.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: The man who approached them and asked about inheritance.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who later explains why a firstborn gets no double share of a mother's property.

terms.meaning: The Torah gives a firstborn son twice the share of each other son in his father's estate.
A method of reading in which two things mentioned together in a verse are taken to share the same rules.

09.note: The Sadducees held that a daughter inherits together with a son's daughter. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai confronted them: fools, where do you get this? No one could answer except an old man who chattered that if a son's daughter inherits, the man's own daughter surely should. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai cited verses about Zibeon and Anah to show grandchildren count as children. The Sadducee said, Master, you dismiss me with this? Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai called him a fool and broke his argument: a son's daughter is stronger because she inherits beside her father's brothers, while a daughter is weaker, since she does not inherit beside her brothers. The Sages won, and made that day, the twenty-fourth of Tevet, a festival.
09.why: The Gemara has been setting the order of heirs, with a son's descendants ahead of a daughter. Rav Huna, quoting Rav, calls the opposite view a Sadducee practice, and this account from Megillat Ta'anit is his proof.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage who argued against the Sadducees.

people.name: An old man
people.about: The one Sadducee who offered an argument.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Sage who answers an objection to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's proof from Genesis.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: In another version, the Sage who gives that answer.

terms.meaning: A Jewish group of the Second Temple period who rejected many of the Sages' traditions.
An ancient list of minor festivals, days on which fasting and eulogies were not allowed, marking happy events.
An argument from a weaker case to a stronger one: if something holds in the lesser case, all the more so in the greater.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

10.note: A dying man said: my property goes to my grandmother, and after her to my heirs. He had a married daughter, who died while her husband and the grandmother were still alive. After the grandmother died, the daughter's husband claimed the property. Rav Huna said "my heirs" includes the heirs of his heirs, so the husband takes it; Rav Anan said it does not. A ruling was sent from the Land of Israel: the law follows Rav Anan, that the husband does not inherit, but for a different reason. The property was only due to the daughter, never held by her, and a husband does not inherit what is only due to his wife.
10.why: Abaye and Rabba have been arguing over whether a firstborn gets a double share of debts owed to his father, and Abaye mentioned this case in passing. The Gemara stops to explain it in full.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Ruled the daughter's husband should inherit.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: Ruled the husband should not inherit.

terms.meaning: Property one is only due to receive in the future, as opposed to property one already holds; a husband inherits his wife's holdings but not what was only due to her.

11.note: A firstborn son sold his own share and his dead brother's share of their father's property before the estate was divided. The dead brother's orphaned sons went to eat dates from the field, and the buyers hit them. The orphans' relatives protested that the buyers had bought their property and were now beating them too. They came before Rava, who said the firstborn had done nothing: his sale was void. Rav Pappi and Rav Pappa later disagreed over whether Rava meant only the brother's share or the firstborn's extra share as well.
11.why: The Gemara has been debating whether a firstborn owns his extra share before an estate is divided. It reveals that the dispute between Rav Pappi and Rav Pappa was never stated outright but inferred from Rava's ruling in this case.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Judge who ruled the firstborn's sale invalid.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: Read Rava's ruling as voiding only the brother's share.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Read Rava's ruling as voiding the whole sale.

terms.meaning: A firstborn son receives a double share of his father's estate; the question is whether it is his before the brothers divide the estate.
A son who is not the firstborn and takes a single share.

12.note: Rabbi Yehuda the baker said this happened to his sister's daughter, who was also his daughter-in-law: her husband had written her a deed giving her all his property, and then a debt against him came to light. The case came before the Sages. They said she must tear up her marriage contract and keep the deed of gift, which the creditor could collect from, so she was left bald on both sides.
12.why: The Gemara is asking whether a healthy man who writes all his property to his wife truly gives it to her. A baraita and Rabbi Yehuda's case are cited as a possible proof that he does, but the Gemara rejects it, saying it may concern a dying man.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda the baker
people.about: Reports what happened to his niece, who was married to his son.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, a document guaranteeing a wife a sum from her husband's property if he dies or divorces her.

terms.term: Bald from here and from there
terms.meaning: An idiom for losing on both counts: she got neither the gift nor her marriage payment.
A document recording a debt, which lets the lender collect from the borrower's property.

13.note: Yosef ben Yo'ezer had a son who did not behave properly, so he consecrated a vessel full of dinars to the Temple instead of leaving it to him. The son married the daughter of King Yannai's crown weaver. When his wife gave birth, he bought her a fish and found a pearl inside. She told him not to sell it to the king's treasury, which would pay little, but to the Temple treasurers, and to let them set the price. They valued it at thirteen vessels of dinars but had only seven; he took seven and consecrated the other six. The treasurers wrote that Yosef ben Yo'ezer brought in one and his son six; others say they wrote that the son took out seven.
13.why: The mishna says one who leaves his sons nothing is disliked by the Sages, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel praises it when the sons behave badly. The Gemara tries this story to see whether the Sages disagree with him, but the two versions point opposite ways, so nothing is proved.

people.name: Yosef ben Yo'ezer
people.about: Father who consecrated his money rather than leave it to his badly behaved son.

people.name: His son
people.about: Found a pearl in a fish and sold it to the Temple.

people.name: His son's wife
people.about: Daughter of King Yannai's crown weaver; advised him how to sell the pearl.

terms.meaning: Given to the Temple treasury, so it belongs to the Temple.
Officials who managed the Temple's funds.
The rule that a promise to the Temple binds at once, as fully as handing an item to a person, so a low price once named could not be taken back.

14.note: A man whose children did not behave properly wrote all his property over to Yonatan ben Uzziel. Yonatan sold a third, consecrated a third to the Temple, and gave the last third back to the man's children. Shammai came to him with his staff and bag to protest. Yonatan said: if you can take back what I sold and what I consecrated, you can take back what I returned; if not, you cannot take that back either. Shammai said: ben Uzziel has rebuked me, ben Uzziel has rebuked me.
14.why: The Gemara is asking whether it is right to cut children out of an inheritance; Shmuel has just warned against it. This story shows a Sage who received such a gift and gave part of it back to the children.

people.name: Yonatan ben Uzziel
people.about: Received the man's property and returned a third to his children.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: Came to protest Yonatan's returning part of the gift.

terms.meaning: Given to the Temple treasury, so it belongs to the Temple.

15.note: In Beit Horon, a man's father had vowed to take no benefit from him. When the man was marrying off his own son, he told a friend: the courtyard and the wedding meal are given to you as a gift, but only so that my father can come and eat with us. The friend replied: if they are mine, they are consecrated to Heaven. The man said he had not given them so the friend could consecrate them. The friend answered that the gift was only a way for father and son to eat, drink and make peace, with the sin of breaking the vow hanging on his head.
15.why: The Gemara asks why Shammai first protested Yonatan ben Uzziel's handling of a gift, and answers that he had this case in mind. From it the Sages ruled that a gift the receiver could not consecrate is no gift.

people.name: The son
people.about: A man of Beit Horon whose father had vowed to take no benefit from him.

people.name: The friend
people.about: Received the courtyard and meal as a gift and declared them consecrated.

terms.meaning: A binding vow forbidding someone to get any benefit from another person, including eating his food.
Declared the property of the Temple, which forbids anyone else to use it.

16.note: A woman had a palm tree on Rav Beivai bar Abaye's land, and every time she came to harvest it he got angry with her. So she transferred the tree to him for all the years of his life. He then transferred it to his young son. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said to him: because you come from a cut-short family, do you say cut-short things? Even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows such a sale only when the property was to pass to someone else afterward, not when it was to return to the giver.
16.why: Rava has just ruled that a gift given on condition that it be returned is still a real gift. This case explores the limits of such a gift, which goes back to the giver after a set time.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: Owner of the land where the woman's palm stood; received the tree for his lifetime.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Sage who rejected Rav Beivai's transfer to his son.

people.name: A certain woman
people.about: Owner of the palm tree, who gave it to Rav Beivai for his lifetime.

terms.meaning: A wordplay: Rav Beivai's family traced its line to Eli, whose descendants were cursed with early death, so Rav Huna calls his reasoning cut short too.

17.note: A man told his wife, before she had conceived: my property goes to the sons I will have with you. His older son from an earlier marriage came and asked: and what will become of me? The father told him: go and acquire like one of those sons. The Gemara notes that the unborn sons certainly acquired nothing, since they did not yet exist.
17.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a fetus cannot acquire property given to it. This case of a gift to sons not yet conceived follows, and the Sages then argue over whether the older son got anything extra.

people.name: A certain man
people.about: Promised his property to the sons he would have with his wife.

people.name: His older son
people.about: Son from an earlier marriage who asked what he would receive.

18.note: Rav Safra's father left him money, and Rav Safra took it and went into business with it. His brothers took him to court before Rava, claiming a share of the profits. Rava told them: Rav Safra is a great man; he would not leave his studies to toil for others.
18.why: The mishna rules that heirs who said from the start that they are trading with their own share keep the profit. Rava's ruling shows that a man like Rav Safra is treated as if he had said so, even without saying it.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Invested the money his father left and was sued by his brothers.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Judge who ruled the profits were Rav Safra's.

19.note: Rav Yehuda, in Shmuel's name, told of a man who sent his father-in-law's house a hundred wagons of wine and oil, a hundred of silver vessels, a hundred of gold vessels and a hundred of fine wool garments. He rode over in his joy and stood at the entrance; they brought out a cup of a hot drink, he drank it, and he died. Rabbi Aha Sar HaBira raised the case before the Sages in Usha, and they said that gifts meant to be used up are not returned, and those not meant to be used up are returned.
19.why: The mishna says a betrothed man who ate a groom's feast at his father-in-law's cannot reclaim his gifts, and the Gemara asks whether drinking counts. It reads this case as proof that drinking does.

people.name: A certain man
people.about: A betrothed man who sent great gifts and died at his father-in-law's door.

people.name: Rabbi Aha Sar HaBira
people.about: Brought the case before the Sages in Usha.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, which binds the couple before the wedding when they begin to live together.
Gifts a betrothed man sends to his bride's family; the question is when they must be returned if the marriage does not happen.
A town in the Galilee where the Sages met as a court.

20.note: Rav Yehuda, in Rav's name, told of a man who heard that his betrothed had lost her sense of smell. He followed her into a ruin, carrying a date, to test her. He said: I smell the scent of radish in the Galilee. She said: who will give us of the dates of Jericho to eat, showing she had smelled his date. The ruin fell on her and she died. The Sages said that since he went in after her only to test her, he does not inherit from her.
20.why: It follows another incident Rav Yehuda reported in Rav's name, in the Gemara's discussion of what a betrothed man and his bride's family owe each other when a betrothal never becomes a marriage.

people.name: A certain man
people.about: A betrothed man who tested his bride's sense of smell.

people.name: His wife
people.about: His betrothed, who was killed when the ruin collapsed.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage; a betrothed couple are legally bound but have not yet begun married life, and the man does not inherit from her.
